name: PA12 (Nylon 12)
chemical_makeup: Aliphatic polyamide homopolymer from laurolactam — eleven methylene carbons between amide groups against PA6's five. The long hydrocarbon run dilutes the amide (hydrogen-bonding) content, which is the single fact behind every difference from PA6: less moisture uptake, lower density, lower melting point, more flexibility.
summary: The calm, forgiving nylon. Deltas vs the base pa entry: moisture absorption under 1 % against PA6's 3-9 %, so drying drops to 70 °C / 4 h instead of 12 h and redrying between prints is often unnecessary; density falls to 1.01 g/cm³ (the lightest polyamide here, ~7 % more part volume per kilo than pa6); elongation exceeds 50 % and HDT@0.45 MPa reaches ~135 °C. It pays for that with lower stiffness (tensile ~45 MPa vs PA6's 55-58) and a higher price. Vs siblings: much easier and far more humidity-stable than pa6 or pa66, and a completely different hardware class from ppa.

printing.notes: Nozzle window matches the base pa entry (Fiberlogy specifies 255-270 °C for its unfilled PA12; eSUN's ePA12 spans 240-290 °C), so the delta vs pa6 is not temperature but tolerance: PA12 shrinks and warps less, so the enclosure is about draft exclusion rather than rescue. Bed runs at the top of the base range, ~110 °C per Fiberlogy. Part cooling stays near zero as for all nylons — this material needs a warm, still chamber, never open-door cooling, so enclosure_open_for_cooling is false. Unfilled PA12 is not abrasive; the pa12-cf sibling is (0.4 mm+ hardened nozzle, 265-285 °C, layer height >=0.25 mm).

feeding.notes: Rigid but noticeably tougher and less brittle than pa6 or pa66, so it survives a material station's bend radii better than any other nylon here — snap risk in the buffer is the lowest of the family. No shore hardness and no feeding assistant (not an elastomer); any extruder feeds it. Rated 'conditional' rather than 'yes' only because it is still a polyamide: use a sealed, desiccated unit. The moisture argument is weaker than for pa6 though — with <1 % absorption, PA12 tolerates an unsealed feed path for far longer than its siblings. Third-party fiber-filled PA12-CF remains barred from standard AMS units on fibre-wear grounds (unverified brand by brand).

drying.dryness_validation: No popping, crackling or steam at the nozzle and a glossy, void-free purge line; stringing back to baseline on a retraction test. Because PA12 absorbs so little, a spool that has been sealed with desiccant usually passes this check with no drying at all — which is the practical test that distinguishes it from pa6.
drying.notes: The clearest differentiator in the polyamide family. Fiberlogy specifies 70 °C for 4 h against Bambu's 80 °C for 8-12 h on PA6 grades, and 3DXTech puts PA12's moisture uptake below 1 % against PA6's 3-9 %. required_before_use is therefore 'if-exposed' rather than the base pa entry's 'always' — the only polyamide in this catalog that earns that. The pa12-cf sibling still wants 90 °C / 4-6 h if it has been out in the room.

storage.recommendations: Sealed with desiccant is still the right default, but PA12 forgives a lapse: a spool left out overnight is usually still printable, where PA6 would already be bubbling. Keep humidity under 30 % and re-dry only if a purge line pops or strings.

price.notes: Meaningfully above pa6: Fiberlogy's unfilled PA12 runs ~EUR 48 for 0.75 kg (~$68/kg), and specialist PA12 grades span $55-90/kg. The base PA12 resin simply costs more than caprolactam-derived PA6, which carries through to the filled grades too — 3DXTech's CarbonX PA12-CF was listed at $88/500 g (~$176/kg), though it was out of stock at the time of checking and that figure should be re-verified.

recommended: parts exposed to oils, fuels, hydraulic fluid and solvents
tubing, wire sheathing and cable protection
functional prototypes that must hold size across humidity swings
outdoor-adjacent mechanical parts where pa6 would swell
not_recommended: maximum-stiffness tooling in a controlled dry environment — pa6 or pa66 is stiffer and cheaper there
budget projects (the most expensive unfilled nylon in this catalog)
parts needing pa66's wear resistance and low creep

properties.notes: Density 1.01 g/cm³ (Fiberlogy) is the lowest polyamide figure in the catalog and sits below the base pa entry's grade-averaged 1.08 — 100 g of PA12 yields 99 cm³ against pa6's 88.5, an ~12 % volume advantage per kilo. Tensile at yield 45 MPa with modulus 1400 MPa and elongation at break >50 % — softer and far more ductile than pa6 (55-58 MPa), which is the core stiffness-for-toughness trade. Charpy impact 12 kJ/m². HDT@0.45 MPa 135 °C is well above pa6's ~85 °C, but Tg ~40 °C is the lowest here, so the material creeps under sustained load long before HDT — read HDT as short-term deflection resistance, not a service ceiling. Shrinkage is a reasoned reduction from the base entry's 1.0-2.5 % consistent with PA12's low-warp reputation, not a datasheet figure.

compatibility.notes: Welds to itself and to the aliphatic polyamide family, though the PA12/PA6 and PA12/PA66 interfaces are weaker than same-grade bonds because the melting points differ by 40-80 °C. No bond to pla, petg, abs, asa, pc, pp, pctg, pvb or pet. Same-material breakaway supports are the default, but PA12 is the one grade in this family with a documented soluble option: 3DXTech lists AquaTek X1 USM as compatible with its PA12-CF, so a water-soluble interface is worth testing here where it is a non-starter for pa6/pa66. pva still degrades below the print range.

plate_recommendations.notes: Upgraded from the base pa entry's 'usable': PA12's lower shrinkage means edge lift is far less of a threat, and Fiberlogy lists smooth or textured PEI with adhesive (or glass plus adhesive) as normal practice. A glue stick is still applied as an adhesion promoter, and it doubles as a release layer against over-bonding on smooth PEI. Garolite / G10 is not the near-requirement here that it is for pa6 and pa66 — no such plate entry exists in the catalog yet, so this is recorded in notes.

emissions.notes: Rated a step below pa6 and pa66 on VOCs: PA12 is laurolactam-based, so it is not a caprolactam source, and the characteristic acidic nylon odour is milder. General nylon fume and ultrafine-particle concerns still apply above ~250 °C nozzle, so source-capture extraction or a HEPA+carbon filter is recommended for long jobs. No PA12-specific emissions study was found — this is the general nylon-family guidance applied with the monomer difference accounted for (unverified).

safety_notes: Keep drying below 90 °C. Molten PA12 in the hotend behaves like any nylon — do not clear a clog by hand at temperature. The pa12-cf sibling adds respirable carbon-fibre dust during sanding or machining; wet-sand and wear respiratory protection there. Not food-contact suitable: FDM layer crevices harbour bacteria regardless of the polymer's industrial food-grade status.
additional_notes: PA12 is the grade to reach for when the part has to hold its size in an uncontrolled environment. 3DXTech's own PA6-CF vs PA12-CF comparison makes the trade explicit: PA6 wins on dry stiffness and HDT (175 °C vs 150 °C on their filled grades) but those numbers degrade as the part takes up water, while PA12's stay put — so PA6 wins the datasheet and PA12 wins the shop floor. PA12 also anneals less dramatically than PA6, since there is less moisture-driven property swing to recover.

provenance.conflicts: HDT is the widest disagreement: Fiberlogy's unfilled PA12 cites 135 °C @0.45 MPa while the base pa entry records 80 °C as a PA6/PA12 midpoint and unfilled PA6 is commonly listed at 55-85 °C — the gap is real (PA12 grades genuinely test higher) but 135 °C sits oddly against a Tg of ~40 °C, so treat it as short-term deflection rather than a service ceiling. Nozzle range differs by vendor (Fiberlogy 255-270 °C vs eSUN ePA12 240-290 °C). Moisture uptake '<1 %' is 3DXTech's figure with no measurement condition stated. Price for PA12-CF ($176/kg equivalent) was taken from an out-of-stock listing and needs re-verification. UV tolerance is scored above pa6 on dimensional-stability grounds rather than intrinsic photostability — no UV-exposure test data was found for unfilled PA12 (unverified).
